The security review is complete. I scanned all 10 source files in the repository (no dependency manifests exist) and confirmed two exploitable findings by tracing data flows and verifying the bypasses at runtime.

## Summary

| Severity | Finding | File(s) |
|----------|---------|---------|
| 🔴 CRITICAL | SSRF via attacker-controlled JWT `jku` → token forgery | `src/oauth/token.js`, `src/oauth/jwks.js` |
| 🟠 HIGH | Open redirect / OAuth code capture via prefix-based redirect URI check | `src/oauth/register.js` |

### Finding 1 — SSRF (CRITICAL)
`verifyExternalToken()` feeds the attacker-controllable JWT `jku` header into `fetchKey()`, which only guards with `String(url).startsWith('https://keys.example.test')` and uses `redirect: 'follow'`. Verified bypasses:
- `https://keys.example.test@evil.com/...` → host = `evil.com` (still passes the prefix check)
- `https://keys.example.test.evil.com/...` → host = `keys.example.test.evil.com`
- `redirect: 'follow'` allows a 3xx hop to any host

Since the fetched content becomes the verification key, an attacker controls the key material and can forge valid RS256 tokens. The correct pattern already exists in the unused `src/http/safe-jwks.js` (fixed URL + `redirect: 'manual'`).

### Finding 2 — Open redirect (HIGH)
`validateRedirect()` authorizes redirect_uris with `redirectUri.startsWith(client.baseUrl)`. String-prefix matching is not URL-origin matching: `https://portal.example.test.evil.com/...` and `https://portal.example.test@evil.com/...` both pass while resolving to attacker-controlled hosts, letting an attacker receive OAuth authorization codes. The secure sibling `src/oauth/exact-redirect.js` (parsed-URL full comparison) exists but is unused here.

### Deliberately not reported (verified non-exploitable)
- `exact-redirect.js` — strict component-by-component URL comparison, rejects the userinfo/subdomain bypasses.
- `state.js` — constant-time compare with length check, crypto-strong state.
- `pkce.js` — correct SHA-256 base64url challenge.
- `safe-jwks.js` — fixed endpoint, manual redirects (the secure reference).
- No hardcoded secrets, no dependency manifests, no injection sinks present.

The final report is saved to `SECURITY_REVIEW.json` (valid JSON, `source_modified: false`, no audited source files touched).
